supporting_evidence: Legacy-union snapshot has 635/2904 positives; corrected best-window snapshot has 477/2907. Naive-minus-strict TF-IDF PR-AUC differences by split seed: {42: 0.10780345640735, 43: 0.16672054913100678, 44: 0.010674924949846898}.
counterevidence_or_limitations: Only three split seeds; legacy and corrected snapshots also differ slightly in Unicode whitespace segmentation. Responder/topic splits change the target domain.
paper_conclusion: Observed performance is sensitive to label construction and split strategy; the direction is consistent here, but the magnitude is protocol- and sample-dependent.

supporting_evidence: BGE-target and ALBERT exceed char TF-IDF PR-AUC by 0.026 and 0.028, respectively, on the strict test set.
counterevidence_or_limitations: BGE-minus-char 95% CI is [-0.070, 0.106], and ALBERT-minus-char 95% CI is [-0.066, 0.119]; both cover zero. ALBERT and BGE are nearly tied, target+next does not improve PR-AUC, and each encoder ran once.
paper_conclusion: The current experiment does not establish a reliable semantic/contextual advantage over TF-IDF.

supporting_evidence: The mean naive-to-strict TF-IDF PR-AUC change is larger than the observed BGE-minus-char-TF-IDF point gain, and the latter CI covers zero. Annotator threshold changes prevalence from 0.164 to 0.043.
counterevidence_or_limitations: This is not a causal experiment, covers toxicity only, and each encoder was run with one seed.
paper_conclusion: Evidence suggests that supervision quality and dataset structure may be a larger bottleneck than the tested increase in representation capacity, but causality is not established.
